metadata.title: Data Sufficiency for Simple Interest
metadata.description: Decide whether one statement, the other, either one, both together, or neither can uniquely determine a simple-interest quantity.
metadata.teachingApproach: Treat sufficiency as a uniqueness test, not a calculation contest. Start with missing P/R/T cases, then include either-alone and both-needed patterns, split-capital equations, three-statement redundancy, and a capstone where two equations still do not uniquely determine the requested variable.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 22, Simple Interest (printed pp. 641–662). Approved scope: Teach the chapter's five-outcome two-statement data-sufficiency format and extend to three-statement combinations. Use rate, principal, amount, doubling, split-investment, and interest-difference situations. Emphasise testing I alone, II alone, and only then both; distinguish redundant information from genuinely independent equations; and flag cases where multiple P,R,T combinations remain possible.

content.text:
Data Sufficiency for Simple Interest

Decide whether one statement, the other, either one, both together, or neither can uniquely determine a simple-interest quantity.

We will build the idea with small numbers first, then move into the exam-style patterns from the chapter.
Data Sufficiency asks a different question: not 'what is the answer?' but 'do I have enough information to get one unique answer?' Test Statement I alone, then II alone, then both only if needed.

To find a rate, knowing only total interest is not enough; knowing only time is not enough. Even together, interest and time still leave principal unknown. That is an 'insufficient even together' case.
Find the S.I. rate. I: total interest is ₹4000. II: time is 4 years.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Find the S.I. rate. I: total interest is ₹4000. II: time is 4 years.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: Rate needs S.I., P, and T.
I+II still do not give P.
inlineData.explanation: Neither statement gives principal, so even together they cannot determine the rate.

content.text:
The key clue is this:

Rate needs S.I., P, and T.

Neither statement gives principal, so even together they cannot determine the rate.

Now try the same idea with fresh numbers.
Find the S.I. rate. I: S.I. is ₹900. II: principal is ₹6000 and time is 2 years.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Find the S.I. rate. I: S.I. is ₹900. II: principal is ₹6000 and time is 2 years.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives interest only.
II gives P and T only; together all three are known.
inlineData.explanation: Both statements are necessary: together R = 900×100/(6000×2).

content.text:
Work through this version once:

Both statements are necessary: together R = 900×100/(6000×2).

Keep the same reasoning and try it again.
A statement can be sufficient by itself if it fixes all needed relationships—even if it never gives the principal explicitly.
If an amount doubles in 10 years, S.I.=P and RT=100. So rate is 10% immediately. A second statement about rupee interest would be unnecessary.
Find the rate. I: The amount doubles in 10 years at S.I. II: Interest in 5 years is ₹5000.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Find the rate. I: The amount doubles in 10 years at S.I. II: Interest in 5 years is ₹5000.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: Statement I gives RT=100 with T=10.
Statement II lacks principal.
inlineData.explanation: I alone gives R=10%. II alone cannot determine R.

content.text:
The key clue is this:

Statement I gives RT=100 with T=10.

I alone gives R=10%. II alone cannot determine R.

Now try the same idea with fresh numbers.
Find the rate. I: S.I. equals 30% of principal in 6 years. II: S.I. is ₹1800.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Find the rate. I: S.I. equals 30% of principal in 6 years. II: S.I. is ₹1800.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives RT/100=0.30.
II lacks P and T.

content.text:
Work through this version once:

I alone gives R = 30/6 = 5%.

Keep the same reasoning and try it again.
Sometimes each statement alone is sufficient. That is different from 'both are necessary'. Always test them separately before combining.
If I says a sum doubles in 8 years, rate is fixed. If II independently says S.I. is 40% of principal in 4 years, rate is also fixed. Either statement alone works.
Find the rate. I: A sum doubles in 8 years. II: S.I. is 50% of principal in 4 years.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Find the rate. I: A sum doubles in 8 years. II: S.I. is 50% of principal in 4 years.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives R=12.5%.
II also gives R=12.5%.
inlineData.explanation: Either statement alone determines the same rate, so answer is 'either alone'.

content.text:
The key clue is this:

I gives R=12.5%.

Either statement alone determines the same rate, so answer is 'either alone'.

Now try the same idea with fresh numbers.
Find the rate. I: A sum trebles in 20 years. II: S.I. is 75% of principal in 7.5 years.

II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

options.label: I alone is sufficient

Either I or II alone is sufficient

I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives R=10%.
II gives R=10%.

content.text:
Work through this version once:

Each statement alone determines R=10%.

Keep the same reasoning and try it again.
A statement about amount often needs one more piece. Amount alone mixes principal and interest; combine only if the missing variable is supplied.
If I says ₹8000 becomes ₹8800 and II says the time is 2 years, principal is already visible in I, interest is ₹800, and II supplies time. Together the rate is fixed.
Find the rate. I: ₹8000 becomes ₹8800 at S.I. II: the time is 2 years.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Find the rate. I: ₹8000 becomes ₹8800 at S.I. II: the time is 2 years.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives P and S.I., but not T.
II gives T; together R is unique.

content.text:
The key clue is this:

I gives P and S.I., but not T.

Both are needed. R = 800×100/(8000×2) = 5%.

Now try the same idea with fresh numbers.
Find the principal. I: Amount after 3 years is ₹6900. II: Rate is 5% p.a.

II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

I and II together are necessary

hints: Together A,R,T are known.
inlineData.explanation: Both statements are necessary to solve P = 6900/1.15.

content.text:
Work through this version once:

Both statements are necessary to solve P = 6900/1.15.

Keep the same reasoning and try it again.
In split-investment sufficiency, ask whether the statements create enough independent equations for the unknown parts.
If total capital is known but only one rate is known, that is not enough. If total yearly interest is also known and the second rate is known, the split becomes unique.
How much of ₹12000 is at 6%? I: the rest is at 9%. II: total yearly interest is ₹900.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: How much of ₹12000 is at 6%? I: the rest is at 9%. II: total yearly interest is ₹900.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives both rates but not the split.
II gives one interest equation; with I it becomes solvable.

content.text:
The key clue is this:

I gives both rates but not the split.

Both are necessary: 0.06x + 0.09(12000−x)=900.

Now try the same idea with fresh numbers.
How much of ₹10000 is at 5%? I: the rest is at 8%. II: overall yearly rate is 6.2%.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: How much of ₹10000 is at 5%? I: the rest is at 8%. II: overall yearly rate is 6.2%.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives the component rates.
II gives total interest = 6.2% of ₹10000.
inlineData.explanation: Together they determine the split uniquely.

content.text:
Work through this version once:

Together they determine the split uniquely.

Keep the same reasoning and try it again.
If the target is a principal, a statement giving the rate and another giving an amount at a known time can work together. But a relationship that still contains two unknowns may remain insufficient.
The sufficiency test is about uniqueness, not about having many numbers on the screen.
Find principal P. I: P earns ₹1200 S.I. in 3 years. II: rate is 8% p.a.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Find principal P. I: P earns ₹1200 S.I. in 3 years. II: rate is 8% p.a.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives S.I. and T.
II supplies R.
inlineData.explanation: Together P = 1200×100/(8×3). Neither statement alone is enough.

content.text:
The key clue is this:

I gives S.I. and T.

Together P = 1200×100/(8×3). Neither statement alone is enough.

Now try the same idea with fresh numbers.
Find principal P. I: the rate is 8% p.a. II: P earns ₹1600 S.I. in 2 years at 10% p.a.

II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Find principal P. I: the rate is 8% p.a. II: P earns ₹1600 S.I. in 2 years at 10% p.a.

Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives only a rate, no interest or time.
II directly gives S.I., R, and T.
inlineData.explanation: II alone gives P = 1600×100/(10×2) = ₹8000. I alone does not.

content.text:
Work through this version once:

II alone gives P = 1600×100/(10×2) = ₹8000. I alone does not.

Keep the same reasoning and try it again.
For three-statement questions, the same principle applies: look for the smallest sufficient combination and notice redundant information.
If a sum amounts to ₹690 after 3 years and ₹750 after 5 years, those two statements alone give the annual interest and principal. A third statement giving the rate is redundant.
Which is sufficient to find principal? I: amount after 3 years is ₹690. II: amount after 5 years is ₹750. III: rate is 5%. Choose the best description.

options.label: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
Any two of the three
All three are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Which is sufficient to find principal? I: amount after 3 years is ₹690. II: amount after 5 years is ₹750. III: rate is 5%. Choose the best description.

options.label: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
Any two of the three
All three are necessary

hints: I+II use the constant yearly amount difference.
I+III and II+III also each determine P.
inlineData.explanation: Any two are sufficient: I+II find yearly interest and P; either amount statement plus III also fixes P.

content.text:
The key clue is this:

I+II use the constant yearly amount difference.

Any two are sufficient: I+II find yearly interest and P; either amount statement plus III also fixes P.

Now try the same idea with fresh numbers.
Which data are enough to find principal? I: amount after 2 years is ₹6600. II: amount after 5 years is ₹7500. III: rate is 5%.

Any two of the three
All three are necessary

hints: I+II gives yearly interest ₹300 and P ₹6000.
I+III or II+III also solve P.
inlineData.explanation: Any two statements determine the principal.

content.text:
Work through this version once:

Any two statements determine the principal.

Keep the same reasoning and try it again.
Capstone sufficiency questions often hide redundancy. The fastest check is to count unknowns and independent relationships, then verify that the result would be unique.
Knowing only a difference in interest caused by changing rate and another difference caused by changing time can still leave P, R, and T entangled. More equations do not guarantee a unique value.
Find principal P. I: raising the rate by 2% increases S.I. by ₹108. II: increasing time by 2 years increases S.I. by ₹180.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I gives 2PT = 10800.
II gives 2PR = 18000. These determine ratios, not P alone.
inlineData.explanation: There are still multiple P,R,T triples satisfying both equations, so even together the principal is not unique.

content.text:
The key clue is this:

I gives 2PT = 10800.

There are still multiple P,R,T triples satisfying both equations, so even together the principal is not unique.

Now try the same idea with fresh numbers.
Find rate R. I: increasing rate by 2% for the same 3-year term adds ₹240 interest. II: principal is ₹4000.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

inlineData.prompt: Find rate R. I: increasing rate by 2% for the same 3-year term adds ₹240 interest. II: principal is ₹4000.

options.label: I alone is sufficient
II alone is sufficient
Either I or II alone is sufficient
Even I and II together are insufficient
I and II together are necessary

hints: I+II only confirm the rate-change effect; they do not reveal the original rate.
The question asks for original R, not the new rate.
inlineData.explanation: Even together, the original rate can be many values. The information only explains the ₹240 difference.

content.text:
Work through this version once:

Even together, the original rate can be many values. The information only explains the ₹240 difference.

Keep the same reasoning and try it again.

You can now tell whether a simple-interest problem is solvable before doing the arithmetic. That completes Topic 22: from the basic fixed-interest model through changing conditions, investment splits, finance plans, and source-style data sufficiency.
